cells.tense: You are letting go and seeing ahead at the same time, right now, and one is making room for the other.
cells.ask: Feed this next: when a hunch comes, say out loud where it points before you check whether it's practical, then act once on the one that keeps pulling.
cells.core:
You can feel what's not here yet and open to it without flinching. Something gets held loosely enough to let go of, and what moves into the space has a shape you can almost touch. You're not managing that. You're doing it.

What keeps this working is genuine engagement, not effort. Wanting what you're feeling sustains it; forcing it drains it. So notice when imagining turns into a way of holding on, and set that picture down with the same hands you use for the rest. Letting go and sensing want the same abandon, and the direction they point is yours to name. Let your sense of what's next choose what's next, and let what you've finished with keep moving out.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go and knowing what's next at the same time.
cells.verb: Sensing what is coming and giving it shape with wide-open attention
cells.place: Standing where you let go of what you're done with, so there's room for what isn't here yet

cells.tense: You are living a step ahead of a future that hasn't happened, bracing for how it will feel, and the straining is costing the thing it's for.
cells.ask: Picture one outcome you're braced for, then put it down by doing one small real thing today that doesn't depend on it.
cells.core:
You can sense a possibility so vividly that it starts to feel like a plan. You build for how it will go, rehearse the feelings of something that hasn't arrived, and treat your own picture as if it has authority over events. The bracing feels like care. It's mostly gripping.

None of this needs solving by imagining harder. What's here is soft enough already: spend today tending one real, ordinary thing — not the scenario in your head, the houseplant, the person across the table, the pot on the stove. Growth that happens without forcing it keeps the vision safe too. You don't have to stop picturing ahead. Let something else hold the rope, and the picturing stops pulling so hard.

cells.tense: You have stopped letting a vision arrive, and the pictures you keep working with are ones you made earlier.
cells.ask: Name one practice you've quietly let go of, then do it once today — one rough run only, no drafting it well.
cells.core:
When it's working, a picture arrives and you take it in with wonder — not because you forced it, but because you meet what's new without a grip on it. That openness is the part that's missing. The pictures you have are the ones you already know, and you keep picking them up instead of meeting anything fresh. Nothing new gets felt.

The picture doesn't have to be good, and pushing harder won't turn this around. Put a plain question to one person: what's something you've put off picturing — a trip, a room, a change in what you do? Say it out loud, even badly. One rough run, today.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what comes next while telling yourself you're only keeping up with what's in front of you.
cells.ask: Take a hunch you wrote off as a lucky guess and write its next step down with a date on it.
cells.core:
The sensing is running. Hunches land and they hold. You feel a room before you walk into it, sense how a conversation will go before it starts. You work from that, and the account you give is that you're keeping things practical and you'll figure out the rest when you get there.

What happens is you wait for the pull to show itself before you call it yours. Name one hunch you've already acted on as a guess about yourself, whether it worked out or not, and stop hedging it. Sensing what's coming doesn't need more discipline. It needs you to sign the work, the way your own hand moves when you score a page without noticing.
